title: Ribociclib + endocrine therapy · metastatic

agents.name: Ribociclib
agents.explanation: Ribociclib blocks CDK4 and CDK6, proteins that help cells move through the cycle of division. Endocrine therapy reduces the hormone signal that can drive HR-positive breast cancer.
agents.watch: Keep blood and ECG appointments. Fever, jaundice, fainting, palpitations, severe rash or new breathlessness need prompt advice.
risks: Rare serious lung or skin reactions

agents.name: AI or fulvestrant
agents.explanation: An aromatase inhibitor (AI) lowers oestrogen production; fulvestrant blocks and reduces oestrogen receptors. These are alternative endocrine partners, selected by the team. Ovarian suppression is needed in pre/perimenopausal patients.
agents.watch: The endocrine medicine continues during the ribociclib week off. Report troublesome joint, menopausal or injection-site symptoms.
risks: Hot flushes, joint pain and fatigue
Bone loss with AI / ovarian suppression

purpose: Ribociclib with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant aims to control advanced HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. The exact endocrine partner depends on previous treatment and menopausal status.
schedule_summary: Ribociclib is taken once daily on Days 1–21, followed by seven days off, in a 28-day cycle. The endocrine partner continues according to its own prescription. Treatment continues while it is helping and tolerable.

phases_note: A general pathway, not an appointment calendar. Your team confirms the order, overlap and duration; no date entry is needed.
timeline_note: Treatment bands show the source schedule. Symptom bands show possible patterns, not measured probabilities; serious effects can occur at any time.
safety_note: Fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell require immediate contact. Serious symptoms override the timeline or diary.
teachback: Can you explain the current phase, which checks are expected next, and which symptoms mean you should call today? You do not need to enter dates to read the plan.
consent_support: Discuss the treatment aim, alternatives, expected benefit, serious and lasting risks, fertility/pregnancy precautions, the planned monitoring and who to contact. Review the full longitudinal pathway and confirm which conditional treatments apply.
urgent_extra: Report new breathlessness, chest symptoms, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, jaundice, a painful swollen leg or a severe rash promptly. You do not need to identify which medicine caused the symptom.

support.title: Three weeks on, one off
support.text: The ribociclib break is Days 22–28. Your endocrine partner usually continues.

support.title: Bloods and ECG
support.text: Early blood tests and a Day-14 ECG are important even if you feel well.

support.title: Medicines check
support.text: Avoid grapefruit; check new prescriptions, over-the-counter medicines and supplements for interactions.

support.title: Missed or vomited tablets
support.text: Do not take an extra dose. Take the next prescribed dose at the usual time and contact the team if uncertain.

questions.q: How does this fit around surgery and radiotherapy?
questions.a: Ribociclib is taken for three weeks of each four-week cycle with endocrine treatment. The first two cycles need extra blood checks and an early ECG; cancer-response reviews continue over the longer term.

questions.q: Do I need to enter dates?
questions.a: No. Both charts explain the expected sequence and general intervals without any dates or personal information. Your hospital arranges actual appointments.
The treatment journey lists baseline and ongoing checks, why they matter and what to ask. It does not mark tests as booked or completed.

questions.q: What happens if treatment is delayed?
questions.a: Your team may delay, reduce, change or stop a medicine. Ask which component changes and what happens to the next review; do not restart independently.

questions.q: What about fertility, pregnancy or breastfeeding?
questions.a: Discuss fertility preservation and reproductive plans before treatment. The team should explain contraception and breastfeeding restrictions for every medicine, including how long precautions continue afterwards.

questions.q: How should I use trial numbers?
questions.a: Trial results describe groups with defined eligibility. Ask how well those patients and their treatment match your situation; the figures are not an individual prediction.

evidence.title: MONALEESA-2: ribociclib with letrozole
evidence.intro: The treatment setting, trial population and endpoint matter when interpreting benefit.
evidence.population: The phase III trial enrolled 668 postmenopausal women receiving initial treatment for HR-positive/HER2-negative advanced breast cancer.
evidence.interpretation: Median overall survival was 63.9 versus 51.4 months. A median describes a group midpoint, not a personal time limit. This comparison is for ribociclib with letrozole; it must not be relabelled as the fulvestrant or premenopausal trial result.

items.title: Why this regimen?
items.text: Ribociclib with an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant aims to control advanced HR-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer. The exact endocrine partner depends on previous treatment and menopausal status.

items.title: The larger pathway
items.text: Ribociclib is taken for three weeks of each four-week cycle with endocrine treatment. The first two cycles need extra blood checks and an early ECG; cancer-response reviews continue over the longer term.

items.title: ECG: an electrical heart tracing
items.text: Before starting and around Day 14 of cycle 1; then as indicated. Ribociclib can alter the QT interval, which affects heart rhythm. Attend the early ECG and report fainting, palpitations or new dizziness promptly.

items.title: Bloods and electrolytes
items.text: Bloods every 2 weeks for cycles 1–2; before cycles 3–6; then as indicated. Checks blood counts, kidney/liver tests and minerals relevant to heart rhythm. Ask who checks the results before the next pack starts.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Ask for support that fits your priorities.

items.title: Know the continuing plan
items.text: The planned break applies to ribociclib, not automatically to the endocrine partner. Follow the written prescription for each medicine; do not make up missed or vomited doses.

items.title: Keep reporting symptoms
items.text: New or lasting symptoms need assessment between appointments and after treatment stops. Ask for a written summary of continuing medicines, follow-up tests and the contact plan.

steps.title: Before starting
steps.text: Confirm the exact tablet strength, endocrine partner, blood-test and ECG plan where relevant.

steps.title: At home
steps.text: Take tablets whole at the prescribed times. Abemaciclib is continuous twice daily; ribociclib has a planned 7-day break. Follow the schedule for this card only.

steps.title: If a dose is missed or vomited
steps.text: Do not double up or take a replacement dose. Follow the medicine instructions and ask the oncology pharmacist if uncertain.

steps.title: Before the next supply
steps.text: Confirm symptoms and required test results have been reviewed. Ask whether the prescription changes; do not restart a held medicine yourself.

details.title: Interactions and storage
details.text: Check all new medicines and supplements with oncology/pharmacy, avoid grapefruit, store as labelled and keep away from children. Return unwanted tablets to the pharmacy.

details.title: Endocrine and ovarian-suppression visits
details.text: An aromatase inhibitor is generally a daily tablet. Fulvestrant, when selected for metastatic treatment, has loading injections on Days 1, 15 and 29 then monthly. Ovarian-suppression injections have their own prescription and visit schedule.

details.title: No infusion pump
details.text: The CDK4/6 medicine is taken orally. An implanted port or infusion pump is not required for these tablets; other treatment may have separate access needs.

anatomy: Hair loss or thinning varies. Ask about support and scalp cooling where appropriate.
Painful ulcers or difficulty eating and drinking need advice.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment.
Fainting, chest pain or severe breathing difficulty: urgent help. Keep scheduled cardiac checks.
Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor fluid intake, pain or fever.
Report lasting numbness, painful joints or difficulty with daily activities.
Fever, shivers or suddenly unwell: contact oncology immediately.
Severe rash, blistering or yellow skin/eyes needs prompt advice.
